text: 9:40 a.m. The warehouse operations lead messages the team: the inventory sync flow is stuck again, and orders are backing up because stock levels aren't updating. The flow calls an external inventory system through an IntegrationHub action to reserve stock, then updates the order. Nothing in its configuration has changed recently. "Stuck" could mean two very different things, so the investigation starts exactly where it should.

Open the flow's run history and find the execution tied to this order. The current step isn't an approval — this flow doesn't have one — it's the Reserve Stock REST action, and its status reads Error, not Requested or Pending. That single fact answers the first question immediately: this flow has genuinely failed at a specific step, not paused on something waiting to be actioned. A real investigation is justified.

The error message on that step reads HTTP 503, Service Unavailable. On its own that's informative, but the integration's own structured checkpoint log — the same gs.error pattern from course 7 — has an entry at the same checkpoint, with the same transaction ID, the same 503, and a matching timestamp. Two independent sources agreeing on a 503 is far stronger evidence than either alone.

This is where the bug-versus-external fork earns its keep. A 503 isn't a 401, which would point at the Connection and Credential Alias. It isn't a 429, which would point at call volume. A 503 is the signature of an outage — the external inventory system itself isn't responding normally. The Script Performance Profiler confirms it: almost no time was spent building the request, and the response came back fast with a rejection, not a slow timeout.

Checking the vendor's own public status page confirms a listed incident starting nineteen minutes before the first failed run. That closes the loop — this is external, not a ServiceNow bug, not a credential problem. The right move isn't editing the flow or the script, since neither is broken. It's telling the warehouse lead specifically what's happening: the inventory system is down, confirmed independently, the platform is working correctly, and retries will pick runs back up once the vendor recovers.

Had the team started by editing the flow instead of checking the execution log first, they'd have spent real time changing working logic while the actual cause sat entirely outside their instance. Checking status, then the specific code, then an independent source is what turns a vague complaint into an accurate explanation of what's happening and who actually needs to fix it. Next, in Chapter Six: triaging a slowdown across the whole platform, not just one flow.
